label: Person
name: Adolf of Nassau-Wiesbaden-Idstein
summary:
Adolf of Nassau-Wiesbaden-Idstein (c. 1423–1475) was Archbishop of Mainz from 1461 to 1475, one of the most turbulent archiepiscopates in the history of that great see. The Archbishopric of Mainz was the premier ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire — its archbishop was the Arch-Chancellor of Germany and the presiding Prince-Elector at imperial elections — making it the most powerful church office in the German world. Adolf's path to the archbishopric was itself contested, arising from a disputed election that was only resolved through papal intervention.

Adolf's archiepiscopate coincided with the later phases of the Gutenberg revolution: Johannes Gutenberg had produced his famous Bible in Mainz by 1455, and the printing press was beginning to transform European intellectual life. As Archbishop of Mainz in this pivotal decade, Adolf presided over the city that was the birthplace of European printing, even as he managed the military and political conflicts that characterised his reign.

His tenure was marked by the ongoing conflict between the Nassau and Isenburg families for control of Mainz's electoral chapter, as well as complex negotiations with the emperor and the city's merchant class. His management of the archbishopric's finances and military resources reflected the heavy demands placed on German prince-bishops who had to function simultaneously as secular rulers, military commanders, and spiritual leaders.
